paper_title: UniRestorer++: Scalable Universal Image Restoration with Multi-Granularity Degradation Modeling

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Universal image restoration aims to handle diverse degradations within a single model, but a reliable scaling strategy remains underexplored. Increasing backbone depth and width can lead to performance saturation, while degradation-aware specialization depends on accurate degradation estimation and is vulnerable to errors on out-of-distribution and real-world inputs. We propose UniRestorer++, a scalable framework based on multi-granularity degradation modeling. It progressively refines degradation groups and introduces group-specific experts, coupling capacity growth with specialization. Degradation-estimation-based routing selects a root-to-leaf path, while granularity-estimation-based routing chooses a level along that path to balance specialization and robustness. Spatially dense degradation representation maps further enable region-aware routing for spatially non-uniform corruptions. We develop CDD-50, a benchmark covering 50 degradation categories from single to penta-degradation. Experiments show approximately log-linear PSNR trends over the evaluated model-size range and stronger scaling gains on out-of-distribution and real-world data than vanilla MoE scaling. UniRestorer++ achieves state-of-the-art performance across benchmarks and demonstrates zero-shot generalization and few-shot transfer on real-world images. Code: https://github.com/mrluin/UniRestorer_plusplus

sections.content: 1 UniRestorer++: Scalable Universal Image Restoration with Multi-Granularity Degradation Modeling Jingbo Lin, Zhilu Zhang, Fan Li, Renjing Pei, Wenbo Li, Hang Xu, Hongzhi Zhang, and Wangmeng Zuo AbstractUniversal image restoration aims to handle diverse degradations within single model. Despite rapid progress, reliable scaling strategy remains underexplored. The conventional strategy of simply increasing backbone depth and width can exhibit performance saturation, with optimization conflicts across restoration objectives remaining potential bottleneck. Degradation-aware methods allocate specialized capacity, but finer specialization requires more accurate degradation estimation and becomes vulnerable to estimation errors, especially on out-of-distribution and real-world inputs. To this end, we propose UniRestorer++, scalable universal image restoration framework driven by multi-granularity degradation modeling. Specifically, we construct degradation hierarchy for model scaling by progressively refining the degradation group and introducing group-specific restoration experts, thereby coupling capacity growth with degradation-specific specialization. To ensure reliable scaling, degradation-estimation-based routing selects root-to-leaf path within the hierarchy, while granularity-estimation-based routing selects an appropriate level along that path, balancing fine-grained specialization with robustness against degradation-estimation errors. Furthermore, spatially dense degradation representation maps enable regionaware expert routing to adaptively handle spatially non-uniform corruptions. We develop the CDD-50 benchmark, encompassing 50 degradation categories ranging from single-degradation to penta-degradation. Extensive experiments show approximately log-linear PSNR trends over the evaluated model-size range, with stronger scaling gains on out-of-distribution and real-world data than vanilla MoE scaling. UniRestorer++ achieves stateof-the-art performance across comprehensive benchmarks. It also demonstrates zero-shot generalization and few-shot transfer capability on real-world images. The code and pre-trained models will be publicly available at https://github.com/mrluin/ UniRestorer plusplus. I. INTRODUCTION MAGE restoration aims to recover high-quality visual content from degraded observations, supporting applications in computational photography [1], medical imaging [2], remote sensing [3], autonomous driving [4], and security surveillance [5]. Early methods were typically tailored to individual degradations, e.g., DnCNN [6] for denoising and SRCNN [7] for super-resolution. As degradations diversified and neural architectures advanced, research expanded from task-specific methods to task-agnostic restoration backbones, including MPRNet [8], SwinIR [9], Restormer [10], NAFNet [11], and X-Restormer [12]. More recently, universal image restoration has emerged to address multiple restoration tasks and diverse degradation types within single unified model. Representative universal image restoration frameworks. Fig. 1. (a) Degradation-agnostic methods use shared backbone without explicit degradation conditioning. Degradation-aware methods guide restoration through conditioning (b) or expert-based processing (c) that routes features toward degradation-specific experts. These representative methods typically use fixed degradation granularity, which can make them sensitive to degradationestimation errors. (d) UniRestorer++ proposes multi-granularity degradation modeling, expanding model capacity by introducing finer degradation-specific restoration experts. Degradation-estimation-based routing determines hierarchical path, while granularity-estimation-based routing selects an expert level along that path, balancing degradation-specific specialization with robustness to degradation-estimation errors.

sections.content: restoration methods can be broadly categorized into degradation-agnostic and degradation-aware methods. Degradation-agnostic methods jointly train shared backbone on data across all tasks (see Fig. 1(a)), but conflicting restoration objectives (such as denoising and deblurring) can hinder restoration quality. Degradation-aware methods use degradation information to guide restoration and can be further divided into conditioning-based and expert-based approaches. Conditioning-based methods use learnable prompts [13][16], degradation representations [17], [18], or adapters [19] to modulate shared restoration backbone (see Fig. 1(b)). Expertbased methods allocate degradation-specific capacity through specialist models [20], [21], selective filters [22], [23], lowrank adaptation (LoRA) experts [24], routing features toward specialized pathways (see Fig. 1(c)). Despite rapid progress in universal restoration, existing methods still exhibit noticeable performance gap compared to specialist models, particularly when confronted with an expanding and diverse degradation space. Drawing inspiration from advances in large language models [25], [26] and largescale vision models [27][29], scaling up the capacity of universal restoration models represents promising direction to close this gap and potentially surpass specialist models. However, simply increasing the depth and width of dense restoration network yields limited gains in our experiments (see the 2 Fig. 2. To reduce parameter interference, degradation-aware methods use conditioning or expert specialization to adapt restoration processing to different degradation subspaces. Nevertheless, the efficacy of these methods critically hinges on degradation estimation, where the finer parameter specialization required for model scaling demands higher estimation accuracy. For out-of-distribution and real-world degradations, degradation-estimation errors can activate mismatched parameters and compromise the benefit of increased specialization (see Vanilla MoE Scaling in the lower part of Fig. 2). In this paper, we argue that scalable universal restoration framework must ensure that capacity expansion effectively translates into both predictable performance and generalization gains. Achieving this goal fundamentally requires scaling up the model while maintaining robustness against degradation-estimation errors. To address these challenges, we present UniRestorer++, scalable universal image restoration framework driven by multi-granularity degradation modeling, as illustrated in Fig. 1(d). First, we construct degradation hierarchy to govern the capacity scaling of universal restoration models. Each subsequent hierarchy level refines the degradation space of the preceding level into finer groups and introduces groupspecific restoration experts for the resulting subspaces. The expansion of model capacity is thereby achieved by increasing the depth of this hierarchy. Second, while deeper hierarchies provide more specialized capacity, they can also amplify the consequence of degradation-estimation errors. To enable reliable scaling, we employ multi-granularity expert routing mechanism that balances expert specialization with robustness against degradation-estimation errors. Specifically, finegrained experts specialize in narrow degradation subspaces, whereas coarse-grained experts cover broader distributions to improve robustness under ambiguous estimates. Degradationestimation-based routing determines root-to-leaf path within the hierarchy, while granularity-estimation-based routing selects an appropriate level along that path. For instance, an ambiguous estimate of heavy snow can be routed to coarsegrained general-snow-removal expert, whereas confident estimate can activate fine-grained heavy-snow-removal expert. Third, existing methods generally use an image-level degradation representation to condition restoration, without explicitly selecting different experts for individual spatial locations. However, haze density, blur patterns, and many realworld degradations often vary spatially. To address this issue, our method predicts spatially dense degradation representation maps for region-aware expert routing, allowing different experts to be selected for distinct regions in an image. We conduct extensive experiments across multiple evaluation settings. We develop the CDD-50 benchmark, which encompasses 50 distinct degradation categories ranging from single corruptions to complex mixtures of up to five simultaneous degradations. Experimental results demonstrate that UniRestorer++ consistently establishes state-of-the-art performance across in-distribution, out-of-distribution, and realworld degradation benchmarks. Crucially, the proposed hierarchical model scaling strategy exhibits approximately log-linear PSNR trends over the evaluated model-size range, with steeper fitted slopes than vanilla mixture-of-experts (MoE) scaling on out-of-distribution CDD-50 and FoundIR, as shown in Fig. 2. By scaling the parameter capacity up to 2.9B, we establish the largest known fidelity-oriented universal restoration model, which demonstrates fine zero-shot generalization and few-shot transfer capabilities on real-world images.

sections.content: this work was published in the Proceedings of ICLR 2026 [31]. Methodologically, the present manuscript extends the original multi-granularity routing mechanism into scalable universal restoration framework by establishing hierarchical model scaling method and generalizing global routing to spatially adaptive expert routing. Empirically, this work constructs comprehensive CDD-50 evaluation benchmark, while providing investigations of scaling behavior, out-of-distribution generalization, and few-shot transferability. The contributions are summarized as follows: We propose hierarchy model scaling method for universal image restoration, which progressively refines the degradation partition and assigns restoration experts to the resulting subspaces. We propose multi-granularity expert routing mechanism, which balances expert specialization with robustness against degradation-estimation errors. We present region-aware expert routing scheme, allowing local regions to dynamically activate distinct restoration experts for spatially non-uniform degradations. We establish the CDD-50 benchmark encompassing 50 degradation categories. Extensive experiments characterize the empirical log-linear scaling trend over the evaluated model-size range and demonstrate superior performance in universal restoration, real-world zero-shot generalization, and few-shot transferability. II. RELATED WORK A. Image Restoration for Specific Degradations Early image restoration methods developed architectures tailored to individual degradations, e.g., DnCNN [6] for denoising, SRCNN [7] for super-resolution, DeblurGAN-v2 [32] for deblurring, PReNet [33] for deraining, Dehazeformer [34] for dehazing, and DesnowNet [35] for desnowing. Advances in deep architectures produced general-purpose restoration backbones, including MPRNet [8], SwinIR [9], NAFNet [11], Restormer [10], and X-Restormer [12]. These backbones can be trained separately for different restoration tasks and provide specialist baselines. B. Universal Image Restoration Overview. Universal image restoration aims to process multiple known or unknown degradation types within single model. Existing approaches fall into two categories: degradation-agnostic and degradation-aware. Degradationagnostic methods share all model weights and learn cross-task knowledge implicitly from mixed training data, which suffer from restoration-task conflicts. Degradation-aware methods instead estimate degradation representations (DRs) and use them as priors, following the paradigm of blind image restoration [36], [37]. Within this category, methods can be further divided into conditioning-based and expert-based approaches according to how the degradation priors guide restoration. Conditioning-based Methods. Conditioning-based degradation-aware methods [13], [14], [16][19] integrate prompting [38], adapters [39], or feature modulation [40] into shared restoration backbone. Such mechanisms can support parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), but their use alone does not imply that the backbone is frozen. TransWeather [14] and AirNet [17], e.g., learn degradation-related embeddings that modulate intermediate features for different corrupted inputs. PromptIR [13] combines prompt learning with Restormer backbone [10], whereas IDR [18] integrates taskoriented prior hubs through learnable principal component analysis and dynamic routing. MiOIR [16] combines explicit and adaptive prompts, while OneRestore [15] learns textaligned restoration. composite-degradation However, the degradation-specific processing they induce can be sensitive to errors in the conditioning representation, especially over wide and complex degradation space. prompts for 3 Expert-based Methods. Mixture-of-experts models have demonstrated conditional processing capability in multi-task learning [41][43]. Expert-based degradation-aware methods implement specialization at different scales, from lightweight degradation-specific modules to full restoration networks. E.g., WGWSNet [23] and ADMS [22] learn specific filters on top of shared backbone. DaAIR [44] uses degradation-aware learner in low-rank regime, Instruct-IPT [45] learns low-rank task-specific weight offsets, and LoRA-IR [24] uses low-rank experts. MoCE-IR [46] learns experts with different computational complexities and receptive fields. At the full-model level, GRIDS [21] groups degradations and trains restoration networks for the resulting groups. The related RestoreAgent system [20] instead uses multimodal language model to select restoration tools and their execution order. Despite this progress, degradation-aware approaches typically select prompts or experts at fixed degradation granularity. Although such selection enables degradation-specific processing, it relies on degradation-estimation accuracy and is therefore vulnerable to degradation-estimation errors. Moreover, many such approaches use image-level degradation cues without explicitly selecting different experts for individual spatial locations. Spatially varying feature responses alone do not provide this form of region-aware expert selection. C. Scaling Universal Image Restoration Models Larger models and training sets have improved capability and generalization in natural language processing and highlevel vision tasks. Beyond dense scaling of model depth and width, sparse MoE models enlarge model capacity while activating only subset of parameters for each input [47][49]. Comprehensive model scaling remains underexplored in universal image restoration. Existing work has improved restoration capacity through higher-capacity backbones [10], [12], [50], pretraining on broader degradation spaces [51], [52], or larger high-quality datasets [53]. GenLV [54] studies scalable unified modeling across wide spectrum of lowlevel vision tasks using three dense model variants from 39M to 211M parameters. Scaling laws have characterized empirical relationships between model capacity and performance in language models [55] and high-level vision models [27], [56]. Routed-model scaling laws additionally distinguish total capacity from active computation [55]. These studies do not directly address how parameters should be organized across heterogeneous image degradations. Consequently, whether universal image restoration exhibits predictable scaling relationship and how parameter organization affects this relationship remain underexplored. III. PROPOSED METHOD We first introduce the basic formulation of model scaling, then compare dense model scaling and vanilla MoE scaling to motivate our hierarchy model scaling strategy. We then detail the components supporting our hierarchy model scaling strategy. The overview of our method is shown in Fig. 4. At each restoration block, the degradation-estimation-based and granularity-estimationbased routers are conditioned on both dense DR priors and the current restoration feature, enabling expert routing to adapt throughout the network. B. Scaling Universal Image Restoration Models Dense Model Scaling Strategy. The conventional dense model scaling strategy expands the parameter count by uniformly increasing the depth and width of shared restoration backbone. Because all degradation tasks share an unpartitioned parameter manifold, scaling intensifies gradient interference and optimization conflicts among contradictory restoration objectives (such as high-frequency detail synthesis versus lowpass noise smoothing). Consequently, the effective scaling exponent decays rapidly as model size increases. Beyond critical parameter scale, multi-task optimization conflicts dominate the optimization trajectory, driving the effective exponent to zero and eventually into negative values, which manifests empirically as performance saturation and subsequent collapse. Vanilla MoE Model Scaling Strategy. Sparse Mixture-ofExperts (MoE) architectures decouple parameter interference by routing visual representations to specialized sub-networks. Let Ptotal denote the total parameter capacity of the network, and let Pact denote the active parameter count. Under fixed active computation budget Pact, the term α2 > 0 represents the theoretical upper-bound exponent achievable through total parameter expansion. In universal restoration, vanilla MoE scaling partitions the degradation space into increasingly fine, disjoint clusters governed by flat router operating at single granularity. However, as Ptotal expands, the candidate expert space proliferates, rendering degradation estimation and expert selection progressively more difficult. In contrast, our hierarchy model scaling strategy enables ambiguous or OOD inputs to fall back dynamically to coarser ancestral experts. By safeguarding expert routing against estimation uncertainties across all scales, hierarchy model scaling preserves the theoretical potential of capacity growth, sustaining high and stable scaling exponent αeff,hier > αeff,vanilla across both in-distribution and out-ofdistribution conditions.

EXPERIMENTS We first describe the datasets and evaluation settings in Section IV-A, followed by the implementation details in Section IV-B. We then compare UniRestorer++ with stateof-the-art universal restoration methods in Section IV-C and analyze the scaling behavior of universal restoration models in Section IV-D. We validate the proposed components through ablation studies in Section V. Finally, we give the limitations and conclusions in Section VI. A. Experimental Setup We consider four universal image restoration settings: the single-degradation setting, the triple-degradation setting, the penta-degradation setting, and the real-world evaluation setting. The details are as follows. Single-Degradation Setting. CONCLUSION AND LIMITATIONS In this paper, we presented UniRestorer++, universal image restoration framework that scales capacity through hierarchical degradation-specific experts. Dense degradation representations and multi-granularity routing enable spatially adaptive expert selection while reducing sensitivity to degradationestimation errors. We constructed CDD-50 and evaluated six variants from 154M to 2.9B parameters, observing approximately log-linear PSNR trends within this range. Our method outperforms the compared universal restoration methods and demonstrates zero-shot generalization and few-shot transfer, surpassing the compared specialist models on 14 of 17 test sets after five-shot fine-tuning. These results support hierarchical capacity expansion as promising approach to scalable universal restoration. limitation is that our degradation hierarchy and expert pool are constructed offline and remain fixed during inference. Inspired by recent work on self-improving agents [91], future direction is to extend this modular framework toward recursively self-improving (RSI) restoration agent. Such an agent could diagnose failures, refine degradation groups, add or update experts, and revise their routing, with proposed changes assessed on held-out data. By learning from the outcomes of its own updates, such an agent could improve both restoration performance and its strategy for refining and expanding the expert hierarchy. This would extend our hierarchy model scaling strategy from predefined capacity expansion toward feedbackdriven improvement, allowing restoration capabilities to evolve with changing real-world degradations.
